What has actually changed vs the previous contract\\n*a) Scope of Licensed Platforms*\\nOld version (per your earlier draft):\\n\\u2022 Licensed Platforms included:\\n    \\u25e6 <http://CrazyGames.com|CrazyGames.com> and its domains / apps\\n    \\u25e6 other WebGL / HTML5 portals\\n    \\u25e6 mobile app stores\\nNew version:\\n\\u2022 Game Order now lists Licensed Platforms as only:\\n    \\u25e6 \\u201c<http://www.CrazyGames.com|www.CrazyGames.com> and all of its domains / apps\\u201d\\n\\u2022 Mobile app stores and other generic platforms are no longer in the Game Order.\\n\\u2022 Annex still defines \\u201cLicensed Platforms\\u201d generically as Portal Site + Publisher\\u2019s mobile app + any platforms in the Game Order, but for _your_ deal the Game Order only names <http://CrazyGames.com|CrazyGames.com> and its domains / apps.\\nNet effect:\\n\\u2022 They removed explicit mobile app store coverage and broad \\u201cother platforms\\u201d from your specific deal.\\n\\u2022 They can still show the game inside their own CrazyGames mobile app, but they cannot publish it as a standalone native app on the App Store / Google Play under this Game Order.\\n*b) Transferability*\\nOld version:\\n\\u2022 License in the Game Order was \\u201cworld-wide, non-exclusive, transferable license.\\u201d\\n\\u2022 Assignment clause let Publisher assign the Agreement to a third party upon notice, while you needed their consent.\\nNew version:\\n\\u2022 License now reads: \\u201cworld-wide, non-exclusive, transferable (with a written consent) license.\\u201d\\n\\u2022 Assignment clause in Annex 2 is unchanged:\\n    \\u25e6 You cannot assign without Publisher\\u2019s prior written approval, not to be unreasonably withheld.\\n    \\u25e6 Publisher may assign to a third party on notice only.\\nNet effect:\\n\\u2022 License transfer now formally requires \\u201cwritten consent,\\u201d but the Agreement does not clearly say \\u201cPartner\\u2019s prior written consent.\\u201d\\n\\u2022 Structural asymmetry in Article 31 is still There.\\n*c) Transition Period and SDK obligations after termination*\\nOld version (per your last review):\\n\\u2022 Transition Period: 6 months.\\n\\u2022 SDK integration: update SDK \\u201cuntil 1 year after termination.\\u201d\\nNew version:\\n\\u2022 Transition Period reduced to 3 months. Publisher may keep the game live for 3 months after expiry or termination, and you must keep delivering services during that period.\\n\\u2022 SDK clause now: \\u201cOn request, the Partner will update the SDK to the most recent version until 3 months after the termination of the Agreement, or, when Partner is not able to do so, make it possible for Publisher to integrate the SDK within the Game(s) itself.\\u201d\\nNet effect:\\n\\u2022 Both the transition tail and the SDK support tail got shorter (6 \\u2192 3 months and 12 \\u2192 3 months).\\n\\u2022 Your core problem remains: you still have mandatory post-termination obligations for a non-trivial period.\\n*d) Everything else*\\nFrom the text, the following areas are essentially unchanged relative to what you complained about earlier:\\n\\u2022 No mid-term termination for convenience (only for cause and end-of-term non-renewal with 3-month notice).\\n\\u2022 Outbound links still fully controlled by them (no carve-out for your website or app store pages).\\n\\u2022 Monetization: they still have exclusive rights over ads and IAP on Licensed Platforms, and Partner may only include IAP with their approval.\\n\\u2022 Indemnity and liability: your warranties and indemnity are still broad and uncapped in the text, their liability cap is still \\u201cfees paid or payable to Partner,\\u201d and There is no reciprocal indemnity for SDK / ad stack.\\n\\u2022 Right of first refusal for \\u201cexclusive Games\\u201d remains in Annex 2, but your Game Order still specifies \\u201cnon-exclusive,\\u201d so it does not apply in practice for this deal.\\n\\u2022 Reporting, self-billing, dispute window and lack of explicit audit rights look unchanged.\\nAnd per the tool instructions:\\n\\n2. I will break down why and how to Push it to the low end.
I am not your lawyer or accountant, so treat this as planning guidance and sanity check, not formal advice.

1. What drives the cost
Key factors that matter for Harmony Games specifically:
1. *Type of company and complexity*
    ◦ Delaware C-corp with investors and a real cap table.
    ◦ Multiple SAFEs / equity holders.
    ◦ Employment / contractor agreements across countries.
    ◦ Multiple commercial contracts (publishers, ad networks, platforms, vendors).
2. More complexity pushes you away from “simple startup dissolution” pricing and into custom work.
3. *Where fees show up*
4.  You are not just paying for “file a dissolution form”:
    ◦ corporate / securities law work.
    ◦ Contract review and termination.
    ◦ Employment and IP issues.
    ◦ Tax and accounting cleanup.
    ◦ Possibly some board / investor process work (consents, releases, etc.).
5. *Your goal*
    ◦ If you want a “clean, defendable shutdown” that future investors and acquirers will not side-eye, you will spend more than the absolute bare minimum.
    ◦ If you are ok with more “duct tape,” you can cut costs, but you increase risk of something biting you later.
2. Rough fee ranges by category
These are order-of-magnitude numbers for a company like yours, using a mix of decent startup counsel + a scrappy accountant, not BigLaw overkill.
A. corporate dissolution & governance: *10k–30k*
Covers things like:
• Board and stockholder approvals.
• Formal dissolution with Delaware, plus any foreign registrations (e.g. NC, CA, WA).
• Handling investor rights, preference stack, and confirming There is no distribution or a small pro-rata distribution.
• Drafting or reviewing:
    ◦ Plan of liquidation / dissolution.
    ◦ Officer certificates.
    ◦ Releases and indemnities where needed.
If everything is organized and you work with current counsel efficiently, you might land around *10k–15k*. If lots of custom questions, messy history, or negotiations, *20k–30k*.
B. Contracts, IP, and “shutting the business off”: *5k–20k*
Includes:
• Reviewing and terminating:
    ◦ publishing deals (Boombit, CrazyGames, etc.).
    ◦ Platform agreements ([ORG_NAME_0308], IronSource, ad networks).
    ◦ Vendor and contractor agreements.
• Cleaning up IP:
    ◦ Making sure all game code and assets are properly assigned to the company, so There is no surprise claim later.
    ◦ Deciding what happens to IP: kept in the entity that will be dissolved, sold, or assigned to founders or a new entity.
• Dealing with licenses (engine, SDKs) and privacy / data issues.
If you have reasonably standard contracts and you are willing to send most termination notices yourself, lawyer time can be *5k–10k*. If There is negotiation, disputes, or an IP transfer / sale, *15k–20k+* is possible.
C. Employment, severance, and international wrinkles: *5k–20k*
You have:
• At least one US employee (WA).
• Contractors or employees in Turkey / Balkans / El Salvador, etc.
Items:
• Drafting or reviewing separation/severance agreements.
• Making sure state and country-specific rules are respected (notice, unused PTO, local labor rules).
• Confirming There are no outstanding claims or obvious liabilities.
If headcount is small and fairly aligned and you keep severance simple, legal review might be *5k–10k*. If you need local counsel in multiple countries or any disputes, *15k–20k+*.
D. Tax, accounting, and filings (non-legal): *5k–15k*
This is not legal fees but you have to budget it together:
• Final federal and state Tax returns.
• Sales tax / VAT cleanups if relevant.
• Final payroll / 1099s / T4s / foreign equivalents.
• Closing books, documenting treatment of remaining assets and liabilities.
A lean setup with a good startup CPA who already knows your books might be *5k–8k*. If There is multi-state, multi-country complexity and messy historical books, *10k–15k+*.
E. Contingency and “stuff you didn’t think of”: *5k–10k*
Even with good planning you will get:
• Extra questions from investors.
• A weird contract clause someone finds late.
• A platform or partner who needs a custom letter.
Having *5k–10k* in reserve avoids getting stuck mid-process.

3. Putting it together
For a harmonygames-like profile (Delaware C-corp, external investors, small global team, several commercial agreements, no massive litigation):
• *Very lean scenario, disciplined, everything clean:*
    ◦ Legal: 15k–25k
    ◦ accounting / tax: 5k–8k
    ◦ Contingency: 5k
    ◦ *Total: ~25k–38k*
• *More realistic “not perfect but not a mess” scenario:*
    ◦ Legal: 25k–45k
    ◦ accounting / tax: 8k–12k
    ◦ Contingency: 5k–10k
    ◦ *Total: ~38k–67k*
• *If things are messy or negotiated (IP sale, disputes, local counsel in multiple countries):*
    ◦ Legal: 40k–70k
    ◦ accounting / tax: 10k–15k
    ◦ Contingency: 10k
    ◦ *Total: ~60k–95k*
If you want a single planning number, I would assume *50k all-in* as a defensible budget, then work aggressively to drive it down.

4. How to Push toward the low end
If you decide to seriously plan for this, concrete things you can do now so fees do not explode:
1. *Organize everything:*
    ◦ Clean cap table and stock / SAFE docs in one folder.
• All major contracts in one spreadsheet with:
        ▪︎ Counterparty
        ▪︎ Term / termination clause
    ◦ Notice period
    ◦ Employment / contractor agreements and any option grants clearly filed.
2. *Standardize the exit pattern:*
• Decide in advance:
        ▪︎ Severance formula, if any.
        ▪︎ End dates and communication plan.
    ◦ What happens to IP.
    ◦ Then ask counsel to just “paper this plan,” not design it from scratch.
3. *Have existing counsel give a scoped quote:*
• Ask for:
        ▪︎ A fixed or capped fee for core dissolution package.
    ◦ Hourly for “extras” like complex negotiations or IP sale.
    ◦ Get at least one alternative quote from a smaller startup firm.
4. *Do founder work where possible:*
    ◦ Draft first pass of partner termination emails.
    ◦ Fill out standard forms where allowed.
    ◦ Only loop counsel for review and the parts that carry legal risk.
5. What I would actually do in your shoes
If you are purely planning, not pulling the plug:
• Mentally earmark *50k* as “shutdown runway” in your long-range model.
• In the next quiet window, email current counsel something like:
    ◦ “If we needed to do an orderly dissolution with no contentious issues and minimal distributions, roughly what ballpark would you expect in fees, and what can we do now to make that lower?”
• Make sure your books and cap table are clean enough that you can actually execute a shutdown without a 3-month archaeology project.

1. What the contract actually does (plain summary)
*Parties and scope*
• Between MAXFLOW BV (CrazyGames) as Publisher and Harmony Games as Partner.

*Licensed Platforms*
Defined very broadly as:
• <http://CrazyGames.com|CrazyGames.com> and its domains / apps
• other WebGL or HTML5 browser platforms
• mobile app stores
So by default this contract covers both web and mobile, not just CrazyGames.
*Revenue share*
• Game Revenue is defined as ad + IAP revenue _after_ deducting: agency commissions, ad serving costs, platform fees, payment processing, and VAT/other taxes.
• Net amount is then split: 40 % Publisher, 60 % Partner.
*Hosting and SDK*
• Technology is “Publisher hosting” for these games, so you give them a full build, they host it.
• You must integrate their SDK, keep it up to date, and, on request, update SDK to the most recent version up to 1 year _after termination_ or make it possible for them to integrate the SDK into the game themselves.
*Game updates and parity*
You must:
• Deliver the game within 6 months.
• Keep the web version “always identical to the latest version” on your own sites and any other platforms.
• Ship updates to them no later than anyone else, fix bugs promptly, and provide reasonable ongoing support.
*Outbound links and monetization*
• You cannot include outbound links in the game (for example to your site or app stores) without their explicit written consent.
• They have the exclusive right to serve ads and IAPs on Licensed Platforms. You can only include IAPs with their approval.
*Term, renewal, and transition*
• Initial term: 1 year starting when the game is released on the Licensed Platforms.
• Automatic renewal for the same period, unless a party gives 3 months written notice before the end of a term.
• After expiry or termination, they _may_ keep the game live for a 6-month “Transition Period” and you must keep providing services and cooperation during that time.
*Termination*
• Both parties can terminate for material breach, insolvency, etc., with cure periods for some items.
• Publisher has extra rights to terminate immediately, without liability, if There is alleged IP infringement, breach of warranties, or breach of your obligations.
• There is _no_ mutual termination for convenience anywhere.
*Liability, indemnity, and IP*
• You give broad warranties that you own all IP, do not infringe, comply with laws, no viruses, high quality, etc.
• You indemnify them for IP infringements, legal breaches, and any claims about game content, with no explicit cap.
• Their liability is capped at “fees paid or payable to Partner under the Agreement” and they disclaim most warranties for their portal.
• They can act in your name to issue takedowns against copycats, but have no duty to litigate.
*Data and marketing*
• Each party is an independent controller for personal data, must comply with GDPR etc.
• You cannot use personal data beyond what is necessary, and cannot promote your own or third-party content on their platforms without their written consent.
*Law and venue*
• Governing law: Belgium.
• Exclusive courts: Leuven, Belgium.
2. Key red flags and items to Push on
A. Platform scope: they are grabbing mobile by default
Problem:
• Licensed Platforms includes “mobile app stores,” and the license is world-wide, transferable, and covers publishing and monetization There.
• Combined with their exclusive right to serve ads and IAP on Licensed Platforms, this pulls mobile into their control unless you carve it out.
Pushback / clarification:
• Restrict the Licensed Platforms to _web only_ for this agreement, for example:
    ◦ “Licensed Platforms: <http://www.CrazyGames.com|www.CrazyGames.com> and other HTML5/WebGL browser game portals. For the avoidance of doubt, this Agreement does not apply to any mobile app store distribution.”
• Or, if you want to allow some mobile experiment later, create a _separate_ mobile addendum with tight scope and your veto on any mobile publishing.
This aligns with your plan to keep mobile separate and talk to other mobile publishers.

B. Transferable license + easy assignment by them
Problem:
• License is explicitly “transferable.”
• Assignment clause lets _them_ assign the whole agreement to a third party with only notification, while you cannot assign without their consent.
This means they can sell or spin out your games’ web rights to another company without your approval.
Pushback:
• Make the license non-transferable except to their owned affiliates, or require your prior written consent for any assignment or sublicensing to non-affiliates.
• Make assignment more symmetric: you can at least assign to an acquirer of Harmony Games without needing their consent.
C. Term, auto-renewal, no convenience exit, plus 6-month transition
Problem:
• Initial 1-year term, automatic 1-year renewals, and you must give 3 months notice before the term ends to stop renewal.
• After any end, they can keep the game live for 6 more months, and you must support it.
• There is no termination for convenience for you at all.
In practice that is a long lockdown. If you miss the 3-month window, you are locked for another year plus up to 6 months of transition.
Pushback:
• Add mutual termination for convenience, for example:
    ◦ “After the first 3 months from launch, either Party may terminate this Agreement for convenience upon 30 days written notice.”
• Reduce the Transition Period or remove it. If you accept any transition, limit it to 30 days, and clarify that:
    ◦ Your support obligation is minimal (no new features, only critical bug fixes).
    ◦ They cannot launch the game on new platforms during the transition.
• If they insist on the 6-month Transition Period, tie it only to expiry of a term, not to early termination for convenience or breach.
This directly reduces the lockdown period you are worried about.

D. SDK and support obligations, including after termination
Problem:
• You must implement and keep their SDK up to date, and on request update it “until 1 year after termination,” or else “make it possible for Publisher to integrate the SDK within the Game(s) itself.”
• You must keep the web version identical to the latest version on all other platforms, deliver updates to them no later than others, quickly fix defects, and answer their questions.
Risks:
• You are on the hook for live-ops style support even when the deal is effectively over.
• “Make it possible for Publisher to integrate the SDK” is vague and could be interpreted as pressure to expose more of your build pipeline or code than you want.
Pushback:
• Limit post-termination obligations: for example, “up to 60 days after termination, best-effort support limited to critical bug fixes, no new SDK integrations.”
• Clarify that you are not required to provide source code or build scripts and that SDK integration will always be done by you at your discretion.
• Relax “always identical” wording so you can test features on other platforms first or maintain a lighter web build.
E. Monetization and outbound links: they control everything
Problem:
• They have the exclusive right to serve ads and IAPs within the game on Licensed Platforms.
• You cannot add Outbound Links or promote your own or third-party content through their platforms without explicit written consent.
Impact:
• You cannot naturally promote your own mobile versions or cross-promote your other games from the web build without their explicit permission.
• Any IAP system in the web version requires their approval and flows through their billing.
Pushback:
• Carve out specific outbound links that are always allowed, for example:
    ◦ “Partner may include links to Partner’s official website, and to Domino Delights and Zombie Match mobile store pages, subject to Publisher’s UX requirements, without separate written approval.”
• Clarify that cross-promotion of your own titles within the game is permitted, provided it does not conflict with their ad inventory.
• If you ever want to test your own IAP stack on web, you need at least a negotiation clause instead of pure veto.
F. Indemnities and liability are very one-sided
Problem:
• Your indemnity is broad and uncapped in the text: IP infringement, data protection, any claims about content, plus breach of warranties.
• Their total liability is capped at “the fees paid or payable to Partner,” and they generally disclaim warranties for their site.
This means:
• Worst-case legal risks related to content, data, or IP are largely on you, while their downside is effectively limited to what they have already paid you.
Pushback:
• Add a reciprocal indemnity from them covering:
    ◦ Their SDK, ad tech, tracking, and any UA / ad network practices on their side.
    ◦ Infringement by their branding or assets, and violations of data protection laws arising from their processing.
• Introduce caps and carve-outs:
    ◦ Cap your indemnity and their liability at a defined multiple of annual fees, with higher caps only for IP or data breaches if needed.
• Tighten the IP warranties so you are not giving absolute guarantees far beyond what is realistic.
G. Right of first refusal on variations (sequels etc.)
Problem:
• The exclusivity clause says that where There is an exclusive game, Publisher has a right of first refusal on variations (sequels, prequels, etc.) under the same terms and conditions.
In this specific Game Order the license is “non-exclusive,” so this clause should not bite now, but it is still sitting There.
Pushback:
• Explicitly state in the main agreement or Game Order that:
    ◦ “The exclusivity provisions and right of first refusal in Annex 2, Article 8 do not apply to this Agreement or to any variations of the Games unless explicitly agreed in a future Game Order.”
This prevents later arguments that you owe them first dibs on sequels.

H. Self-billing, reporting, and audit
Problem:
• They issue self-billing invoices and if you do not object within a short time window, they are deemed accepted.
• Strong offset rights if ad networks fail to pay them.
• No explicit reporting detail or audit rights are spelled out.
Pushback:
• Ask for:
    ◦ Monthly detailed revenue reports by platform, geography, ad network, and ad/IAP split.
    ◦ A clear dispute window of at least 30 days from receipt of a statement, with a defined process.
    ◦ A right to audit or have a third-party auditor review their numbers once per year at your cost if discrepancies above a threshold are found.
I. Governing law and venue
Problem:
• Belgium law, courts of Leuven for any disputes.
If you can live with that, you leave it. If you want less friction:
• Propose arbitration in a neutral venue or at least a less one-sided forum clause.
• At minimum, you can leave this as “not a hill to die on” if your main concern is web scope and lock-in, but be aware of the litigation friction.
3. Priority list given your goals
Given what you said you care about (web only, shorter lockdown, easy exit, control if they disappoint), I would prioritize:
1. *Scope and platforms*: Remove “mobile app stores” from Licensed Platforms and make this a pure web publishing deal.
2. *Term and exit*: Add mutual termination for convenience with 30 days notice after an initial test period, and shorten or heavily constrain the 6-month Transition Period.
3. *Transferability / assignment*: Remove transferability beyond affiliates and require your consent for assignments.
4. *Monetization and links*: Explicit rights to link to and promote your own mobile versions and titles, within clear UX bounds.

**Canceled — Telegram initiative called off (Jan 2026).**

The Telegram/DD mini-app push was discontinued in January 2026. Decision of record: Leonard Hayes, in the **#executives** Slack channel on **2026-01-06**, confirmed "we changed directions and won't be doing telegram anytime soon" — the external Telegram contractor's engagement was terminated that day (final $500 payment approved by Robert). This aligns with the earlier CrazyGames scoping decision (Nov 2025) to **exclude Telegram** from web publishing.

Cancelling this master and all remaining open sub-tickets so the tracker no longer shows an active Telegram build. Completed sub-tasks (ENG-2378 WebGL branch, ENG-2379 MiniApp bot, ENG-2387 Jenkins builds) are left as **Done** since that work actually shipped before the initiative was stopped; everything still open (ENG-2380/2381/2382/2383/2384/2385/2386/2388/2389/2390) is canceled.

**Tracker reconciliation vs merged code — 2026-02-28 (Arthur/CTO).**

Reconciled every UI Optimization sub-ticket against merged PRs in `harmonygames-Games/GameOfDominoes`. Several were stuck in PR/Validation long after the code actually landed (Nov 2025), so I flipped them to Done; others had *no* PR behind them and were moved back to Todo.

**Flipped to Done (merged, verified):**
- Core Game (ENG-2403 → Done): Shop 2410 (PR #1898), Leaderboard 2414 + Quest 2415 (PR #1907), Settings 2417 (#1901), Level-win 2418 (#1902), Level-lose 2419 (#1903) — plus the ones already Done (Splash 2409, Character 2411, Saga 2412, Teams 2413, Profile 2416, Chapter 2420, Tavern 2421, Pre-game 2422, Transition 2423). **Core Game group is fully complete.**
- Mini-Games (ENG-2405 → Done): River Tile 2432, Memory Tile 2433, Tile Dozer 2434, Lucky Drop 2435 (all in PR #1905). **Mini-Games group fully complete.**
- Live-Ops: Nathan's Treasure 2425 (#1895), Axe Arena 2426 (#1908) → Done.

**No code behind them — moved to Todo (genuinely not started; not in review):** Collect&win/Magical Wings 2424, River Rush 2427, Season Pass 2428, Remove Ad 2429, Offers 2430, Rate-us Pop-ups 2431. Daily Gift 2437 left In Progress (no PR yet either). All 7 sit under Live-Ops (ENG-2404), which stays open.

This master (ENG-2401) stays open until the Live-Ops group is either finished or explicitly descoped for the wind-down. Given we're shutting down, the realistic call is to descope the remaining 7 unless one is required for the data handover — flagging for Leonard/Robert.

content.text: Now create the Linear ticket to track the Helpshift move (it's been living only in chat). Marking it urgent since the deadline is today.

input.title: Remove Helpshift from Domino Delights & Zombie Match (replace in-game support with email)
input.description:
Tracking ticket for getting **Domino Delights (DD)** and **Zombie Match 3D (ZM)** off Helpshift. This has been living in Slack (#winddown) and wasn't tracked anywhere — creating this so status is visible for the wind-down / Sunset data handover.

## Decision / context
- Company is winding down. Helpshift service is being terminated. Leonard sent the official termination/non-renewal notice to Helpshift (~Feb 9–10, 2026); Helpshift agreed to cancel without hassle, all outstanding balance paid, and Helpshift is marked done on the wind-down subscriptions tracker.
- Plan of record (Leonard, #winddown, 2026-02-10): replace the in-game Helpshift support flow with a simple "open the email app → email support" flow (send to the DD/ZM support address). No data export from Helpshift is needed.
- Cutoff we set: **end of February 2026 (today, Feb 28)**.

## Status as of 2026-02-28
- **Vendor/account side: DONE** — termination notice sent, cancellation agreed, balance paid.
- **Client/engineering side: NOT STARTED.** Both game clients still ship and initialize the Helpshift SDK and route "Contact Us"/support through Helpshift:
  - DD (`harmonygames-Games/GameOfDominoes`): `HelpshiftInitializer`, `ContactUs.cs`, `TopBarSelectedHero` (unread red-dot), `SupportUS = harmonygames.helpshift.com`. No PR removing Helpshift or adding an email flow (last merged PR in repo is Dec 26, 2025; open PRs are unrelated — Economy changes, Tile Dozer fix).
  - ZM (`harmonygames-Games/match3d`): `SettingsPopup.cs` calls `HelpshiftSdk.ShowConversation`, `SplashScreen` + `SettingsButtonRedDot` use Helpshift, same helpshift Support URL. No removal PR.

**Risk:** if the Helpshift account is shut off before new builds ship, in-app "Contact Us" breaks for live players on both games. The account-side cancellation has run ahead of the client change.

## Remaining work
- [ ] DD: replace Helpshift "Contact Us" with a mailto/open-email-app flow to the support address (include user id in the body, like the existing debug-console mailto). Remove/disable Helpshift SDK init + unread red-dot.
- [ ] ZM: same — swap `SettingsPopup` Helpshift conversation for the email flow; disable Helpshift init + splash/red-dot references.
- [ ] Build + submit updated DD and ZM builds (iOS + Android) so players have a working support path.
- [ ] Confirm final Helpshift account shut-off date with Leonard and sequence it AFTER the new builds are live, to avoid a broken support button in the interim.

• Linear export + Trello export dropped into their shared drive — not delivered yet (no Sunset folder/exports in Drive). I'll own these.

• Publishing agreement *signed early December* (web-only: CrazyGames.com, covers DD + Zombie Match, 60/40 to us). *Integration never started* — no CrazyGames SDK ticket/specs, and the prerequisite economy work (remove lives → tickets) is still an *open, unmerged PR* in DD (#1914, last touched Feb 6). • Economy changes PR #1914 (DD, Lives→Tickets) — open, has unresolved merge markers.

• Live-Ops UI (the 7 above) + CrazyGames integration + Helpshift client removal (ENG-2438) are the real open buckets.

Tickets are all updated in Linear so the exports reflect reality. Shout if you want me to descope the Live-Ops 7 or reprioritize any of this.
